label: Route
description: Turn this program into an HTTP route. A call to the route's path (and method) starts a fresh execution: the request's method, path, parameters, query and headers come out on the fixed ports, and the body's top-level keys come out on the output ports you declare in the source (`-> (user_id: String, text: String)`), exactly like an LLM call with Parse JSON on. Declare every field you read; there is no port for the whole body (a field that is itself an object is `-> (meta: JsonDict)`). A declared port named like a path capture reads the capture (`-> (id: String)` on `cards/{id}`). A port declared as a file kind (`photo: Image`) takes a picture the body carries as a `data:` URL or base64: it is stored on the way in and the stored-file value flows, never the bytes (a value on a wire is at most 100 KB). The whole request body is capped at 256 KB, and a `data:` URL inflates what it carries by about a third, so roughly 190 KB of picture: a caller sending more gets 413 before the run starts, and a page that takes photos resizes them before posting. Answer with a Reply, Stream or Close node downstream, or read the caller through the ctx in a custom node.

inputs.name: path
inputs.label: Path
inputs.description: The route under the project's live URL: literal segments and `{name}` captures (`users/{id}`, `chat/{room}/messages`). Required, and never empty: a trigger with no address would answer at the project's own address, where every other one that forgot would answer too. Must not start with '/'. Two routes of one account may share a call when one spells out what the other captures (`cards/count` beside `cards/{id}`); a pair where neither is the more specific is refused at activation.

inputs.name: method
inputs.label: Method
inputs.description: The HTTP method this route serves. Empty serves every method; a call with another method on a served path is answered 405 by the gateway.

inputs.name: dataType
inputs.label: Body shape
inputs.description: What the body is. `json`: the body parses as JSON and its top-level keys land on the ports you declare, one port per key you want; there is no port for the whole object, so a caller sending anything but an object (a bare list or string) is refused by name. `text`: the whole body is a String on the one port you declare. `bytes`: the whole body is stored as a file and its stored-file value lands on the one port you declare (declare it `File`, or the kind you expect: `Image` for an image upload, which is checked against the file's own bytes and refused if they are something else). The same shape applies to what Reply and Stream send back.

inputs.name: auth
inputs.description: Who may call this route: wire an auth access node (ApiKeyAuth, JwtAuth, HmacAuth). Unwired, the route is open to anyone with the URL. With one wired, the gateway checks the caller before a run starts and the established identity comes out on `caller`.

inputs.name: outlivesCaller
inputs.label: May outlive the caller
inputs.description: Who owns the run, which decides what a caller leaving means. Off (default): the run is the caller's, so their leaving cancels it, and a node that hits a long durable wait holds the worker briefly and is then killed rather than parked. On: the run is its own, so the caller leaving does not touch it and a long wait parks properly and resumes later, making it a background job. Turn it on to answer early and keep working afterwards. Be deliberate about it: the caller leaving is what ends a tied run, so switching this on removes that ending and the work behind the answer must end by itself. Work that finishes on its own (a call, a query, a script) is fine; anything that watches, subscribes or loops until something changes is not, and then you say what ends it, with `maxSessionSecs` here or a TagRun and StopTagged pair in the graph.

inputs.name: defaultHoldSecs
inputs.label: Hold seconds before giving up on a wait
inputs.description: For a caller-tied run: how long a node's wait holds the worker (keeping the connection alive) before giving up. Per-wait overrides win over this. Never unbounded.

inputs.name: maxSessionSecs
inputs.label: Give up on one connection after this long
inputs.description: A hard ceiling on one whole connection, off by default and with no default on purpose: it ends the connection on the clock whatever the caller is doing, so it would cut a healthy live feed short. You rarely want it. A caller who vanishes is already found by `Call the caller gone after this much silence`, whatever the answer is framed as, and that ends the run when the run is the caller's. Reach for this only when it is not: with `May outlive the caller` on, the caller going away no longer ends anything, so a run that would otherwise never finish needs something of its own, and this is the bluntest version of that (stopping older runs by tag is usually the better one).

inputs.name: callerSilenceSecs
inputs.label: Call the caller gone after this much silence
inputs.description: How long the caller's machine may leave what the worker sent it unacknowledged before the connection is called dead, in seconds. This is NOT a ceiling on the call: a machine that is still there acknowledges every packet by itself, whatever the person is doing, so a caller who stays resets this constantly and a run that legitimately lasts hours is never touched. It bounds SILENCE, which is the only way to tell a caller who vanished (a closed laptop, a dropped network) from one who is simply quiet. Raise it for a client on a link that genuinely goes silent for longer, like a device that sleeps its radio between messages; lower it to notice a departure sooner. `0` leaves the machine's own default, which is about fifteen minutes.

inputs.name: journalEphemeral
inputs.label: Keep the exchange out of the journal
inputs.description: What the journal keeps of what was said. Off (default): the request and the answer are recorded, so the inspector replays the exchange and you can see what a caller actually sent. Anything over 100 KB is recorded trimmed, and raw bytes are never recorded whatever this says, so the journal holds what a person would read rather than a copy of the traffic. On: only the sizes and the count are kept, never the content. Turn it on for a route carrying something you would rather not have written down for every run, remembering that you are also giving up seeing it when you debug.

outputs.name: method
outputs.description: The HTTP method the caller used.

outputs.name: path
outputs.description: The path as called under the project (no leading slash), for example `users/42`.

outputs.name: params
outputs.description: The `{name}` captures of the route's path, by name.

outputs.name: query
outputs.description: The query string's parameters, by name.

outputs.name: headers
outputs.description: The request headers, by lowercase name.

outputs.name: caller
outputs.description: Who the auth gate established: a JWT's claims, `{"key": <index>}` for an API key, `{}` for an HMAC. Null when the route has no `auth`.

then.message: Route '{id}' path starts with '/'. The gateway prefixes the route automatically; drop the leading slash.

Route '{id}' starts a run that never answers its caller: no Reply, Stream or Close is in it. Wire the answering node so the run reaches it (through data, or `_should_flow` on the node or on the group it sits in); a custom node answering through the ctx is the one case to ignore this.
